newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Ageing trees cut Nigeria's rubber crop.
newsitem.headline: Ageing trees cut Nigeria's rubber crop.

text.p: Failure to replace ageing trees on smallholder plots is steadily diminishing Nigeria's rubber output, industry sources said.
The Professional Association of Natural Rubber in Africa (ANRA) predicts a crop for 1996 of 90,000 tonnes against 93,000 in 1995 and 95,000 in 1994.
Industry sources said 1997 could be below 87,000 tonnes.
Nigeria is Africa's largest natural rubber producer but it is fighting a reputation for poor quality.

"The reality is that the trend is downwards and the only way to arrest it is through massive replanting and establishment of plantations," Ayoola Fasina, director of the Rubber Research Institute of Nigeria, told Reuters.
Roughly 60 percent of Nigerian rubber is grown by peasant farmers on smallholdings.
The trees are past the 30- to 35-year end of their productive lives and poorly cared for. As production falls, farmers' ability to secure enough capital to replant decreases still further.
"The farmers overtap the trees until they are no longer useful," said Ikay Afe, administrative manager at Michelin, owners of Nigeria's largest estates, told Reuters.
A tendancy to damage trees by burning weeds instead of cutting them and by not paying for chemical inputs was eating further into production.
European Union assistance to help farmers replant was suspended in November after the hanging of author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other minority rights activists for murder, industry sources said.
The only exceptions to the decline are estates of Michelin and Dunlop, which have a local market for rubber at tyre factories and can afford the six- to seven-year wait for trees to mature.
Michelin has just added a new 4,000-5,000 hectare estate to its current 10,000, which should give a total production of 10,000 tonnes a year when trees mature.
"The increased production will serve our tyre factory in Port Harcourt and if world prices look good we will also be able to export," Afe said.
On the world market Nigerian smallholder rubber sells at a discount of up to 20 percent, with a reputation for high moisture content and contamination with foreign matter.
"To increase the weight of the cup lump the farmers have got used to adding bits of wood or metal and factories have played their own part by not insisting on quality," Fasina said.
ANRA is trying to counter this.
"We have already started educating the farmers and buyers, the next step is quality control managers, then by April next year we plan to bring in a quality mark," Fasina said.
"Without the mark, exporting will be impossible."
ANRA predicts that Ivory Coast will overtake Nigeria as Africa's largest rubber producer by the turn of the century.
The civil war which devastated Liberia, formerly the biggest producer on the continent, took production from an annual 108,000 tonnes before 1990 to only around 12,000 tonnes in 1993.
